data:
Michael Samson “Milton” Feller was born on July 29th, 1918 to parents Yitzchak Feller and Rivka Feller (Dominitz). Michael Feller’s parents both came from the Galicia region of Poland, which at the time was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Around 1905, after many of his siblings had been born, his parents moved to New York where they settled for some time. Michael Feller grew up in a large family, having many siblings of vastly different ages. Michael Feller was the youngest in his family, even younger than his nephew, Hyman Katz, who he would later go on to fight in the Spanish Civil War with.

Michael spent his childhood in the East Village, but due to the family being very active in advocating for a Jewish homeland in the Levant, Michael’s father eventually moved to Palestine. He graduated from high school in 1936 and had a stint as a warehouse clerk. Michael would eventually move in with his sister, Leah Katz, at 1550 55th Street in Brooklyn due to his father leaving for Palestine. Following in the footsteps of his many older relatives, he joined the Young Communist League and the Communist Party of the USA. This association would later lead to his interest in the fight against fascism in Spain.

Michael went to Spain in October of 1937, arriving on October 30th, 1937. [1] In Spain, he joined the Spanish Communist Party and Socorro Rojo (International Red Aid). Being in Spain with relatives meant they were often looking out for each other, especially when both Hy and Joseph were wounded and received medical care in April 1938. As the youngest amongst his relatives in Spain they often made it their objective to have him assigned to less dangerous posts, such as topographer and lookout in the 35th Anglo-American Battery division. Doing his training in Almansa, a site noted for its poor organization, it’s doubtless he found himself with less experience than one would hope for.

Throughout the war, Michael kept his hopes high. In April 1938 he wrote, “I needn’t tell you about the Lincoln Brigade and their glorious record. I don’t believe anyone can fully describe their heroism when they resist, attack, or counter-attack.” His Jewish pride was also heightened by the war, where he found many of his fellow volunteers in the International Brigades were also Jewish. In the summer of 1938, Michael was transferred to the anti-tank unit of the 129th International Brigade which he would serve with for the rest of his time in Spain. Though not as cushy as his previous jobs, it was still far enough from the more direct, bloody combat to get him through the war alive. Unfortunately, both Hy and Joseph would not be as lucky, dying during the 2nd Battle of Belchite and the Battle of the Ebro respectively.

Michael would return home from Spain on the SS President Harding in early 1939, and eventually go on to continue the fight against fascism by enlisting in the US army in 1942. Michael would remember his time in Spain fondly, keeping in touch with other Abraham Lincoln Brigade veterans throughout his service in World War II. He appreciated the conditions of the US Army compared to the conditions of the Spanish Republican Army, writing “The food is excellent. We don’t get any ‘garbonzos’ or ‘lentajes’.” In February of 1942 Michael trained at Selfridge Field, Michigan, getting assigned to the Headquarters Squadron of the 3rd Air Base Group, an administrative and logistical role. Michael was then moved to Charleston, South Carolina, to prepare to be transferred across the sea to Europe.

In May, Michael arrived in England, being transferred to the 8th Air Force. While in England, Michael encountered other Spanish Civil War veterans who he connected with, recounting in a letter back home, “Sometime ago while on leave in London I was walking along Piccadilly and a young English lad comes up to me and says --- ‘Hello Mike Feller, what are you doing here?’ It was none other than Fred Langdon --- a vet… He sends his regards to the boys.” Michael was eventually promoted to Staff Sergeant, serving in the 534th Bomber Squadron of the 381st Heavy Bomber Group. Michael was killed in action on October 14th, 1943, over France during the second Schweinfurt Raid also known as Black Thursday. Michael received an Air Medal and a Purple Heart with Oak Leaf Cluster, and is buried in the Lorraine American Cemetery and Memorial in Saint Avold, France.

[1] A photograph at the ALBA archives with Michael Feller suggests that he was in Spain in July of 1937, but I suspect that it is a labeling error on behalf of whoever donated the picture.
